nh_wm_crawford_notch.blurb: A mountain pass on Route 302 in the White Mountains, ringed by granite cliffs. This is chiefly a winter destination: ice is more than half the climbs, mostly WI3 and WI4 with some WI2 and WI5, plus a few mixed lines. On the ice season, Frankenstein Cliff typically runs from late November to early March. Summer brings trad and alpine routes on slabs and buttresses, mostly 5.5 to 5.9, with a few harder. Mt. Willard is a granite cliff with about 300 feet of slab below a 200-foot headwall; Mt. Webster has long slabs facing southwest and west, and the notch also holds Webster Slabs, Elephant's Head and Arethusa Falls. Expect serious, committing terrain with long approaches and quick weather changes higher up.

nh_boulder_natural.blurb: The central bouldering zone of Pawtuckaway State Park in Nottingham, the southernmost of New Hampshire's major climbing destinations. Boulders sit in the forest beside a stream and swamp, and the rock is glacially deposited granite that is smooth yet well textured, with plenty of slopers and crimps, and hard on skin. Every one of the problems is a boulder problem, from V0 to around V11, with the largest numbers in V0 through V4 and a good tail of harder lines. The shady setting means it dries slowly after rain. Autumn is considered the best season at Pawtuckaway, while black flies and mosquitoes are heavy from spring into summer. The Swamp Boulders, The Zoo and The Storm Boulders are the busiest groups.

nh_russell_crags.blurb: Roadside sport climbing near Waterville Valley, on the forested southwest side of Merriam Woods in the town of Woodstock. Trails are loosely marked, so reaching the cliffs takes some navigation. Sport routes make up most of the climbing, with about 40 boulder problems and a smaller number of trad lines. Grades run from 5.7 up through 5.13, concentrated in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, while boulder problems stay mostly between V0 and V6. It is a strong choice for harder sport climbers who want many routes close together. Main Cliff Area, Bird Murder, Y Crag and Roadhouse hold the largest numbers of routes.

or_garden_the.blurb: A bouldering area in the forest near Sweet Home in the Willamette Valley, widely held up as one of the best in Oregon. Several collections of very large boulders sit partly hidden by trees, with moss and dense foliage all around. The stone is generally good, with many rounded slopers, so the crux often comes near the top of the boulder. Problems run from V0 to V11 with a broad spread of grades, and a few cliffs of 30 to 50 feet hold sport routes mostly in the 5.10 to 5.13 range, plus a handful of trad lines. Garden Boulders hold the most problems, then Garden Cliffs, Armageddon and the Clear Cut Boulders.

or_w_the_marsupials.blurb: A remote group of outcrops and towers on the east side of Smith Rock State Park in Central Oregon, reached by a roughly hour-long hike that keeps the crowds thin. Sport climbing dominates by a wide margin, with a small amount of trad. Grades are steep: most routes are 5.10 through 5.13, with the 5.12s the largest group and only a few easy lines. Rock quality varies, and many newer routes still have loose holds. The area has seen heavy new development lately. Marsupial Wall is nearly half a mile of unbroken vertical rock, and Brogan Spire, Koala Rock and Mud Pile add more routes.

wv_darnell_hollow.blurb: A bouldering area in a university research forest near Morgantown, in northern West Virginia's Cheat Canyon country, which is known for gritty sandstone. It holds the densest roadside bouldering in the forest, and its lower elevation keeps it a few degrees warmer than other spots nearby. Nearly everything is a boulder problem, from V0 to V10, with the biggest share between V1 and V4 and a smaller group of hard lines. Landings are mostly flat, and most problems go with pads alone. The 5th Pull Off, 1st Pull Off, Darkside East and Upper 5th Pull Off hold the most problems.
